opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's very feasible. Honestly, it's one of the things I'm most excited about right now. For a long time there was a real worry that interpretability was a toy-model field. You could find a nice circuit in a two-layer transformer, but would any of it survive contact with a model that has hundreds of billions of parameters? I think the last couple of years have pretty convincingly answered that. Techniques like sparse autoencoders and transcoders do scale. The features you pull out of large models are often *more* interpretable, not less, because the model has had the capacity to carve the world up into cleaner concepts.

That said, "feasible" isn't the same as "easy." The bottlenecks change as you go up in scale. A lot of it stops being a research problem and becomes an infrastructure problem. You're capturing activations at enormous volume and training dictionaries with millions of latents. Then you have to serve all of that in a way a researcher can actually poke at interactively. That's a serious engineering lift, and it's a big part of why we've invested so heavily in tooling. You can't do good science if every experiment takes a week to set up.

The other piece is access. If you want to work near the frontier, you need weights, and the strongest models are mostly closed. So there's a real role for strong open-weight models, and for partnerships where interpretability people can work directly with the labs. Some of the most interesting findings only show up at scale: richer reasoning structure, more abstract features, behaviors that don't exist in small models at all. So you really do want to be studying the big ones.

And then there's a research-taste question. At frontier scale, you can't hand-inspect everything. You have to get much better at automating interpretation and at validating that your explanations are actually faithful. And you have to ask "what can I *do* with this?" Can I steer the model, debug a failure, or audit for a behavior I care about? For me, that's the real test of whether interpretability works at scale. It's not whether we get pretty pictures. It's whether understanding the internals lets you do things you couldn't do otherwise. We're increasingly seeing that it does.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because the honest answer a couple of years ago would have been "it's basically not feasible," and I think that's changed in some important ways, but not uniformly.

The core tension is that most of the techniques that make interpretability actually work—sparse autoencoders, circuit tracing, attribution graphs, whatever—were developed and validated on models that are tiny by comparison. GPT-2 small, one- and two-layer toy models, things where you can hold the whole thing in your head, or at least on a single GPU. And the question has always been: does any of this survive contact with a model that has hundreds of billions of parameters, a huge vocabulary, mixture-of-experts routing, long context, all the stuff that makes frontier models frontier models?

And I'd say the answer is "partially, and the parts that don't survive are the parts that matter most."

What does scale fine is the data-side of things. Training a dictionary on activations from a big model is expensive, but it's a known quantity. You throw compute at it, you get features out. Anthropic's work on Claude Sonnet showed you can do that and get features that are genuinely interesting—Golden Gate Bridge, code bugs, sycophancy-adjacent stuff. So the "can we even extract a decomposition" question is mostly solved, if you have the compute and the model access.

What does not scale well is everything downstream of that. Validating features. Understanding what a circuit actually does end-to-end. Going from "here's a feature that activates on X" to "here's a mechanistic account of how the model produces this specific behavior." On a small model you might have a few thousand features and a human can actually look at them. On a frontier model you're at tens of millions, and you cannot have a person look at all of those. So you end up automating the interpretation with another model, and now you've got an interpretability pipeline where the thing doing the interpreting is itself uninterpreted. That's not a dealbreaker, but it is a bit of an epistemic hall of mirrors, and I think people should be more uncomfortable about it than they are.

The other thing I'd flag is access. Frontier-scale interpretability basically requires being inside a frontier lab, or having a very unusual partnership with one. You need the weights, you need the activations, you need an enormous amount of compute just to run the model forward enough times to collect data. That concentrates this research in a handful of places, which has real downsides for the field. The academic work and the open-source community are still mostly doing GPT-2 and Llama-scale stuff, and the question of whether their findings transfer is often just... assumed.

So my overall take: it's feasible in the narrow sense that we can run these methods on big models and get real results. It is not yet feasible in the sense of "we can give you a satisfying mechanistic explanation of why a frontier model did a specific thing in a specific case" at any reasonable cost. And I think the honest framing is that we're racing. Capabilities are compounding fast, and the interpretability toolkit is getting better fast, but I don't think it's obvious which one's winning. If I had to bet, I'd say the techniques will keep working at scale, but the ratio of "stuff we understand" to "stuff the model is doing" is going to keep getting worse for a while before it gets better.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s feasible, but you have to distinguish between studying a frontier model and having a comprehensive understanding of it. Those are very different ambitions. You can make progress on specific questions—what information is represented, which components contribute to a behavior, whether an intervention changes that behavior—without understanding the whole system.

The challenge is that scale makes every part of that process more expensive. You need access to the internals, you need to collect and analyze activations, and you need to run enough experiments to distinguish a compelling story from an actual causal explanation. So access and infrastructure matter a lot.

I’d want a research program that moves between smaller models, where you can iterate quickly, and models close to the frontier, where you can test whether your methods still work. You shouldn’t assume that something demonstrated on a small model automatically carries over. But you also don’t need to solve interpretability completely before doing useful research at frontier scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s feasible, but you have to be precise about what you’re trying to accomplish. Understanding everything a frontier model is doing is a very different goal from understanding a particular behavior or identifying a mechanism that matters for safety.

The practical challenge is that you’re studying a system where even running experiments can be expensive. So you want to develop methods on smaller models, but you also have to test whether the things you’re finding actually carry over. You can’t just assume that a compelling result at a small scale tells you what’s happening at the frontier.

What makes me optimistic is that you don’t necessarily need a complete understanding to get something useful. If you can identify a mechanism, intervene on it, and reliably predict how that changes the model’s behavior, that’s meaningful progress. The key is making that causal connection, rather than just producing an explanation that sounds plausible.
